newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Iraq blocks three U.N. weapons inspection searches.
newsitem.headline: Iraq blocks three U.N. weapons inspection searches.

text.p: Iraq blocked U.N. weapons inspectors from two suspected military sites on Thursday and a third location on Tuesday, U.N. officials said.
"There were instructions from the highest level saying they could not get access," chief inspector Rolf Ekeus said.
He would not name the sites, in the vicinity of Baghdad, but said Iraqi personnel stopped a small group of his inspectors, led by Scott Ritter, an American, on roads leading to the locations.
When they at first refused to move, one Iraqi minder with them said "have a nice day in the sun," Ekeus reported.
Ekeus, head of the U.N. Special Commission in charge of scrapping Iraq's weapons of mass destruction, also wrote a letter to the Security Council on the incidents.
"We are concerned that a decision has been taken by the government of Iraq to prevent full implementation of the commission's mandate," he said.

The letter, obtained by Reuters, said Iraqi officials acknowledged their actions were in violation of Security Council resolutions but "nonetheless confirmed the refusal of access, stating they were doing so on the highest authority."
After the 1991 Gulf War, Iraq was ordered by the council to destroy its ballistic missiles, chemical, biological and nuclear arms. Until then, trade sanctions on oil exports will not be lifted.

The council also said inspectors had to have free rein in conducting surprise visits to search for weapons or documents relating to them. Ekeus has excluded President Saddam Hussein's presidential palaces but not other sites.
Charles Duelfer, the deputy chief of the commission, said the new incidents were "not one of these standoff situations".
This time, he said, "we were told by a high Iraqi official we are not going to get access so the decision was made to withdraw."
Ekeus said the group was searching for concealed items he described only as "tools and documents." He said he would not give details until the team returned to New York next week.
The new disputes followed incidents last week involving alleged interference with U.N. helicopter flights.

According to Ekeus, an Iraqi shut off the fuel pump of one helicopter, manhandled the chief air inspector and a U.N. photographer to prevent them from taking photographs of an inspection site and grabbed pilot controls.

The U.N. flights are to ensure that nothing is removed surreptitiously from sites being inspected by U.N. ground teams. Iraq has challenged the U.N. account of the incidents and said the helicopters were flying over sensitive areas.

Iraq's U.N. ambassador Nizer Hamdoon told reporters there was an agreement with the commission in 1996 that "stresses Iraq's legitimate rights and sovereignty and security and they have to respect that agreement."
He denied Iraqi personnel had endangered the inspectors' lives in the helicopter incidents.
"All they wanted to do was to suggest a different route to the site," he said, adding that the U.N. pilots wanted to fly over sensitive sites and photograph them.
The United States and Britain are arguing that the Security Council issue a stern warning and Chile has been designated to draft a statement, which members are currently considering.
The statement or a possible resolution may be updated in light of the new incidents, diplomats said.
